summary.text: The cross product of two vectors in three-dimensional space is a vector perpendicular to both, written a × b.
Its direction follows the right-hand rule, and its length equals the area of the parallelogram that the two vectors span.
It is the zero vector for parallel vectors, and swapping the order of the two vectors reverses its sign.

facts.label: Dimensions
facts.value: A vector-valued product like this exists only in three and seven dimensions

facts.label: Alternative name
facts.value: Vector product, a name coined by Clifford in 1877

facts.label: Notation
facts.value: Gibbs and Heaviside introduced the cross symbol in 1881

facts.label: Size of result
facts.value: Equals the area of the parallelogram the vectors span

facts.label: Order matters
facts.value: Swapping the vectors gives b × a = −(a × b)

items.prompt: Two vectors point in exactly the same direction. What is their cross product?

options.label: A vector twice as long as either
A vector standing straight out of the page

items.explain: If two vectors are parallel, their cross product is the zero vector.

items.prompt: Two vectors are drawn as sides of a parallelogram. What does the length of their cross product measure?

options.label: The longer diagonal of the shape
The angle between the two sides

items.explain: The magnitude of the cross product equals the area of the parallelogram with the vectors for sides.

items.prompt: Using the right-hand rule, a cross product comes out pointing up. What do you get when you swap the order of the two vectors?
items.explain: The cross product is anti-commutative: b × a = −(a × b).

items.prompt: A game developer wants a cross product that gives a vector, for two vectors in a flat two-dimensional world. What is the problem?

options.label: It is only defined for vectors of unit length
It exists only in three and seven dimensions
It exists in every dimension, but is slow to compute
It needs the two vectors to be exactly parallel

items.explain: The cross product of two vectors is defined only in three-dimensional space, and a vector-valued binary product of this kind exists only in three and seven dimensions.

items.prompt: Point your right forefinger along a and your middle finger along b. Which way does a × b point?
items.explain: By the right-hand rule, the cross product comes out of the thumb. Pointing the fingers the other way round reverses it.

items.prompt: Two arrows meet at a right angle. One is 3 units long and the other is 4 units long. How big is their cross product?
items.explain: The magnitude of the cross product of two perpendicular vectors is the product of their lengths, so 3 times 4.
